findings.claim: Catholic organisations such as the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children (SPUC) and local 'Choose Life' groups campaign against it.
findings.truth: SPUC is not a Catholic body. It is not officially faith-based, although most of its support comes from Catholics and evangelical Protestants. No national Catholic 'Choose Life' group could be verified.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Society for the Protection of Unborn Children: 'Although it is not officially faith-based, SPUC and the more conservative anti-abortion charity Life mainly draw upon Catholic and evangelical Protestant support.'

findings.claim: For 8-mark 'explain two beliefs' questions on this topic, examiners award marks for precise Catholic sources
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. The spec states no mark-scheme rule of this kind, and 'explain two beliefs' is another board's question stem, not this board's.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (lines 3465-3480): the component is described only by time, weighting, marks and compulsory questions; no question stems or mark-scheme wording appear.

findings.claim: Q: 'Which organisation campaigns against assisted dying in the UK?' A: 'Dignity in Dying advocates for it; the Catholic Church and SPUC oppose it.'
findings.truth: The answer leads with the organisation that campaigns FOR assisted dying, so the recall target is the opposite of the question. It also repeats the SPUC mislabel of F1.
findings.evidence: internal check of the flashcard question against its answer

findings.claim: Euthanasia, Evangelium Vitae 65 and palliative care are taught, and the exam tip and the 5-mark practice question make Evangelium Vitae 65 a required source for this theme.
findings.truth: The spec puts euthanasia in the other written paper (Applied Catholic Theology, theme 'Life and Death'). This theme's sanctity-of-life bullet names abortion only. Options: (a) leave the euthanasia material, because 'the origin and sanctity of human life' is the theme's own concept and the teaching is correct; or (b) keep it as background but stop the exam tip and practice mark scheme from making Evangelium Vitae 65 the anchor source here.
findings.evidence: spec lines 3471-3620 (theme content: 'the value of human life, including attitudes toward abortion'); spec lines 217-223 (the other component covers 'Life and Death').
findings.ruling: Leave: low mark risk / unconfirmed iconography.

findings.claim: Remember that spelling, punctuation and grammar carry marks on 15-mark questions
findings.truth: The spec says SPaG is assessed 'in specified questions that require extended writing', worth 6 marks on this paper. It does not say every 15-mark question carries SPaG. The claim is plausible but not confirmed.
Creation from nothing is inferred from Genesis 1:1, not stated there. The explicit scriptural statement is 2 Maccabees 7:28, and the spec anchors the concept in Augustine, Confessions XII, 7.

findings.claim: The fresco depicts the moment from Genesis 1:26-27 when God breathes life into the first human.
findings.truth: God breathing life into Adam is Genesis 2:7, not Genesis 1:26-27. Genesis 1:26-27 is the making of humanity in God's image, with no breath of life. The scene is normally linked to both texts.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, The Creation of Adam: the composition section cites Genesis 2:7 for the giving of life and Genesis 1:26 for the mirrored pose.

findings.claim: affirmed that evolution is "more than just a hypothesis"
findings.truth: The 1996 Message to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences is quoted as 'more than a hypothesis'. The word 'just' is not in the text, and the lesson puts the phrase in quotation marks. Lesson 1 and the lesson 1 knowledge check both use the correct wording.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with L1 n10 and L1 knowledge check 3; standard English rendering of 'plus qu'une hypothese'

findings.claim: That evolution is more than just a hypothesis and is compatible with Catholic faith.
findings.truth: Same misquotation as F8. The recalled phrase must be 'more than a hypothesis'.

findings.claim: The Sistine Chapel as a whole was designed for the conclave in which the Pope is elected
findings.truth: The chapel was built for Pope Sixtus IV between 1473 and 1481 as the Cappella Magna, the pope's own great chapel. It has housed the conclave since 1492; it was not designed for it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Sistine Chapel: 'Originally known as the Cappella Magna... Pope Sixtus IV, who had it built between 1473 and 1481... Today, it is the site of the papal conclave.'

findings.claim: 8-mark question carries the line 'Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.'
findings.truth: That is another board's printed rubric, not this paper's. It is also board rubric pasted verbatim, which the house copyright rule forbids.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section carries no question rubric; house rule in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: 15-mark question carries the bullet rubric 'refer to Catholic teaching / give reasoned arguments to support this statement / give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view / reach a justified conclusion'.
findings.truth: That bullet list is another board's evaluation rubric. This paper's evaluation question asks for a statement to be discussed with more than one point of view, as the lesson 1 question already does.
findings.evidence: internal comparison with the L1 15-mark question; spec assessment section carries no rubric

findings.claim: What do the four Evangelical symbols (man, lion, ox, eagle) represent in Catholic art?
findings.truth: They are the symbols of the four Evangelists. 'Evangelical' means something different and the spec calls them 'the four evangelists'.

1508-1512 is the whole ceiling campaign. The panel itself is dated c.1511-1512. The sentence says the work forms part of the ceiling, so the range is defensible and no correction is safe while sources split between c.1511 and c.1512.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, The Creation of Adam: painted 'c. 1512'; ceiling 1508-1512

findings.claim: The dove - symbol of the Holy Spirit - appears above or near the cross.
findings.truth: The San Clemente cross carries twelve white doves, which the standard reading takes as the twelve apostles, not the Holy Spirit. The spec lists 'dove' among the mosaic's symbols but gives no meaning. Options: (a) leave it, since the dove does mean the Holy Spirit in Catholic art generally; or (b) add that the twelve doves on this cross stand for the apostles. Wikipedia's San Clemente article carries no iconographic detail, so the apostle reading could not be confirmed from an allowed source.
findings.evidence: spec line 3610-3612; Wikipedia, Basilica of San Clemente (no iconographic detail)
findings.ruling: Leave: low mark risk / unconfirmed iconography.

findings.claim: Examiners consistently reward candidates who connect practice to theology rather than giving a purely factual account.
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. Nothing in the spec supports a statement about what examiners consistently do.

CAFOD is the Catholic Agency for Overseas Development. The heading gives a wrong expansion of the acronym, and this lesson's own knowledge check marks 'Catholic Agency for Overseas Development' correct against near-miss distractors.
findings.evidence: spec line 3637 (CAFOD named); L3 body text and glossary; L3 knowledge check 2

findings.claim: 8-mark question carries the line 'Refer to sacred writings or another source of Catholic belief and teaching in your answer.'
findings.truth: Another board's printed rubric, as F11.

findings.claim: 15-mark question carries the same four-bullet rubric as F12.
findings.truth: Another board's evaluation rubric, as F12.

summary: Doctrine, scripture references, Catechism and encyclical paragraph numbers, Vatican II documents, charity founding dates and every knowledge-check and match key are correct across the three lessons. The real damage is in exam-facing text: two fabricated examiner claims, four practice questions carrying another board's printed rubric, a misquoted 1996 papal line, the Creation of Adam attributed to the wrong Genesis verse, a wrong expansion of CAFOD in a heading and SPUC described as a Catholic body.
